plan.chapterName: OpenStax Precalculus 2e, chapter 8: Further Applications of Trigonometry
plan.contextChunk: This figure is a single-panel diagram of a right triangle drawn in the complex plane, with the horizontal axis labeled "Real" and the vertical axis labeled "Imaginary," each drawn as a thin double-headed arrow through the origin. A filled black dot sits in the first quadrant and is labeled "x + yi." A straight segment runs from the origin out to that dot and is labeled r; from the dot a vertical segment drops to the horizontal axis and is labeled y, and the horizontal leg from the origin to the foot of that drop is labeled x, closing the triangle with a right angle at the foot. The angle at the origin, between the positive real direction and the segment r, is marked with a small arc and labeled with the Greek letter theta. A heavier curved arc of constant radius sweeps through the labeled dot and carries arrowheads at both ends, one pointing left beyond the imaginary axis and the other pointing down beyond the real axis, tracing a circle centered at the origin. Laying the rectangular pair x and y and the polar pair r and theta on the same picture lets the reader read either description off the other. The drawing fixes r as the modulus, the distance from the origin to the point, and theta as the direction angle, the two quantities that make up the polar form of a complex number.

interactionPlan.concept: A complex number x + yi can be described equivalently by its rectangular coordinates (x, y) or by its polar form (r, θ), where r is the distance from the origin and θ is the direction angle from the positive real axis.
elements: horizontal axis labeled 'Real', thin double-headed arrow through the origin
vertical axis labeled 'Imaginary', thin double-headed arrow through the origin
filled black dot in the first quadrant labeled 'x + yi'
segment from origin to the dot labeled r
vertical segment from the dot down to the real axis labeled y
horizontal leg from origin to the foot of the drop labeled x
right-angle marker at the foot of the vertical drop
angle arc at the origin between the positive real axis and r, labeled θ
heavier circular arc of radius r through the dot with arrowheads at both ends (one pointing left past the imaginary axis, one pointing down past the real axis)

interactions.label: Angle θ (degrees)
interactions.teaches: The direction angle θ alone determines where the point sits on its circle — as θ changes, the point sweeps around the arc and the x and y legs grow, shrink, and change sign accordingly

interactions.label: Modulus r
interactions.teaches: The modulus r is literally the distance from the origin to the point — changing it grows or shrinks the segment, the circle, and both legs together while the direction stays fixed

interactions.label: Label form
interactions.teaches: Rectangular and polar labels describe the same fixed point — switching annotations changes nothing about the point's position, only which pair of numbers names it

demo_steps.title: One point, two descriptions
demo_steps.narration: The dot x + yi sits at the tip of a right triangle: horizontal leg x, vertical leg y, hypotenuse r, with angle θ at the origin. The same point can be named by (x, y) or by (r, θ).

demo_steps.title: Sweep the angle
demo_steps.narration: Drag θ and watch the point ride the circular arc while x and y update — θ controls direction alone, and the legs are just r·cos θ and r·sin θ.

demo_steps.title: Change the modulus
demo_steps.narration: Now drag r: the segment from the origin, the circle, and both legs scale together while the direction θ stays put — r is visible as distance from the origin, not an abstract label.

demo_steps.title: Same point, polar name
demo_steps.narration: Toggle to polar labels: the point does not move at all. Only the annotations change, emphasizing that x + yi and r(cos θ + i sin θ) are two names for one complex number.

interactionPlan.keyInsight: Rectangular coordinates (x, y) and polar coordinates (r, θ) are two descriptions of the same point, linked by x = r cos θ and y = r sin θ — changing r moves the point radially, changing θ moves it around the circle.
interactionPlan.reconstructionNotes: Complex plane with thin double-arrow axes, 'Real' to the right and 'Imaginary' at top. Draw the point as a filled black dot with its label 'x + yi' beside it; the radial segment r from the origin, the vertical drop y, and the horizontal leg x form a right triangle with a small square right-angle marker at the foot. Mark θ with a small arc at the origin. A heavier blue circular arc centered at the origin passes through the dot, with arrowheads at both ends suggesting the full circle. In rectangular mode show numeric values of x and y next to the legs; in polar mode emphasize r and θ values instead — the geometry stays identical across the toggle. When θ moves into other quadrants, let the legs and labels follow naturally (including sign changes) so learners see the triangle fold across the axes.

plan.authoredInteractions:
- Slider for theta: the learner drags the angle from the positive real axis, the point moves around the circular arc while x and y legs update, and the link between direction angle and rectangular coordinates becomes clear.
- Slider for r: the learner changes the modulus, the segment from the origin and the circle radius grow or shrink with the point, and r becomes visible as distance from the origin rather than a separate label.

authoredContext:
We review these relationships in the figure.

Triangle plotted in the complex plane (x axis is real, y axis is imaginary). Base is along the x/real axis, height is some y/imaginary value in Q 1, and hypotenuse r extends from origin to that point (x+yi) in Q 1. The angle at the origin is theta. There is an arc going through (x+yi).

We use the term modulus to represent the absolute value of a complex number, or the distance from the origin to the point (x,y). The modulus, then, is the same as r, the radius in polar form. We use θ to indicate the angle of direction (just as with polar coordinates). Substituting, we have

discrepancies: The leg labels in the source are plain 'x', 'y', 'r' beside the triangle; the generated figure substitutes computed values ('x = 1.41', 'y = 1.41'), changing the annotation style from symbolic to numeric

The circular arc in the source is a single sweep from the upper-left through the dot to the lower-right of the real axis; the generated arc is offset relative to the point and sweeps a larger loop that dips well below the real axis, with arrowhead tangencies that don't match the source's simple up/left and down arrowheads
The 'r' label is placed very close to the θ angle arc at the origin, making it read as if it labels the angle wedge rather than the hypotenuse midpoint as in the source
The source's θ arc is a clean wedge at the origin; the generated wedge plus nearby 'r' text crowd each other at default θ=45°
evaluation.notes: A strong interactive rendition of the complex-plane polar figure: axes, arc, right triangle with right-angle marker, θ wedge, and dot are all present, and the θ/r sliders plus polar-label toggle are genuinely pedagogical; the main issues are numeric (rather than symbolic) leg labels and an 'r' label crowding the angle wedge.
action_items: Show symbolic 'x', 'y', 'r' beside the legs/hypotenuse as in the source, moving the numeric values to the UI panel or a secondary caption
Reposition the 'r' label to a clean offset beside the hypotenuse midpoint (perpendicular to the segment) so it no longer overlaps the θ wedge
Reduce the arc sweep so it reads as one continuous arc passing through the dot (roughly from the upper-left to below the positive real axis) with arrowheads tangent at its true endpoints
